pos: n. (proper name; a Canaanite people descended from Canaan son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arvadi, the gentilic of Arvad, the island city off the Syrian coast that the Greeks called Aradus. The island is small and waterless, and its men were famous sailors because the sea was all they had.
biblical_def: The Arvadite opens the last line of Canaan's roll: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18), repeated in short form at 1 Chronicles 1:16. Unlike most of the eleven clans, the Arvadite is heard from again. Ezekiel, setting out the merchant glory of Tyre before he sets out her fall, names them twice over: the men of Arvad were Tyre's mariners, and her soldiers manned the walls. “The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners” (Ezekiel 27:8). So the dictionary can say of this clan what it cannot say of the Sinite or the Arkite: here is what they became. They became seamen and mercenaries in the service of the richest city on that coast, and when Ezekiel pronounced the word of the LORD against Tyre, the Arvadite went down with the ship he had rowed. That is the shape of a creature's glory when it is hired out to a creature. The island that bred the best sailors in Phoenicia is named in Scripture chiefly to be listed among the hands that served a city God had appointed to sink.

corruption_summary: Tyre's commercial empire is admired as early globalism; Ezekiel names it as a glory God appointed to sink.
corruption_paragraphs: The Phoenician trading world, in which the Arvadite was a hired hand, is commonly presented as an early triumph of commerce and exchange, with Ezekiel 27 read as an admiring inventory. It is not an inventory; it is a lament, and the lament is a sentence. The chapter catalogues the beauty of Tyre precisely so that the reader feels the weight of the words that follow it, and the dictionary reads it as the prophet wrote it.

The principle to recover is that service rendered to a condemned glory shares its end. The Arvadite rowed well and manned the wall faithfully, and it did not save him, because what he served was appointed to fall. “Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise … shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Ezekiel 27:27). The question Scripture puts to a man's labour is not whether it is skilled but whose it is.

pos: n. (proper name; firstborn son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Almodad, of uncertain meaning; often read as containing the element mdd, to measure, with a prefixed article, hence the measurer. Nothing in Scripture settles it.
biblical_def: Almodad stands first among the thirteen sons of Joktan: “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Genesis 10:26), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:20. Joktan is of the line of Shem through Arphaxad and Eber, which places Almodad in the blessed line — the line out of which Abraham would come — but on the branch that turns away from it. Eber had two sons: Peleg, through whom the promise runs, and Joktan, whose thirteen sons peopled Arabia. Almodad is the firstborn of the branch that does not carry the covenant. Here is the pattern Scripture repeats until a reader cannot miss it. Shem over Ham and Japheth, Peleg over Joktan, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah over his elder brothers, David over seven older sons. Firstborn by nature is not firstborn by election; God has reserved the right of the firstborn to Himself, and He gives it where He will. “The elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). Almodad was his father's eldest and the founder of a people, and the line of promise went the other way.

corruption_summary: Primogeniture is read as the Bible's own rule of inheritance; Scripture overturns it line after line to teach election.
corruption_paragraphs: The genealogies are sometimes read as a straightforward charter of ancient birthright, with the Bible simply reflecting the custom of its age. The text does the opposite with striking regularity. Almodad is a firstborn whose branch carries nothing; Peleg is the brother through whom everything comes. The pattern recurs so often that it is plainly deliberate, and it is deliberate against the custom, not with it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is unconditional election. God's choice is not governed by birth order, merit, or expectation, and the genealogies are where He teaches it before Paul ever argues it. “Not of works, but of him that calleth” (Romans 9:11-12) is the doctrine the lists were written to carry.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Dishon, of the Horite line in Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Keran, of uncertain meaning; possibly connected with a root for a lyre or for lamb, but nothing in the text settles it.
biblical_def: Cheran is named twice, both times last in a short list: “And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Genesis 36:26), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:41. He belongs not to Esau's line but to the Horites, the people who held mount Seir before Edom took it. Genesis 36 is a remarkable chapter: it records Esau's generations, and then, without apology, the generations of the Horites whom Esau's sons dispossessed and absorbed. The dispossessed are written down by name. This is the habit of Scripture that modern reading most often misses. A chapter concerned to show how Edom came to be does not quietly drop the people Edom displaced; it names their chiefs, their sons, and their daughters. Cheran is one such name — a man of a vanished people, preserved in the record of the people who replaced him. “He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations” (Psalm 105:8) is said of God's people; but the God who remembers a thousand generations of His own has not forgotten the Horites either, and He wrote their names in the book that outlasted them.

corruption_summary: Displaced peoples are assumed erased from the biblical record; Genesis 36 enrolls the Horites whom Edom replaced.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often said that the Bible is written only by and for the victors, with the conquered left out. Genesis 36 is a direct counter-instance. The chapter that establishes Edom's pedigree takes a long passage to enroll the Horite chiefs and their sons by name, and Deuteronomy 2:12 states the displacement plainly rather than hiding it. Cheran survives in Scripture because Scripture kept him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the candour of the inspired record. It tells of dispossession it does not flatter, including Israel's own, and it keeps the names of those who lost. A book that preserves the genealogy of a people it reports as destroyed is not propaganda; it is testimony, and its candour is part of why it may be trusted.
